study.title: G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER) modulates epithelial-mesenchymal transition-like phenotype in human glioblastoma cells

cover.headline: A membrane estrogen receptor **drives aggressive behavior** in glioblastoma cells grown in the lab.

slides.title: Glioblastoma is the deadliest brain tumor, and estrogen has been linked to its spread.
slides.body:
The hormone 17β-estradiol can make glioblastoma cells more aggressive by acting through receptors inside the cell. But there's another estrogen receptor—GPER—sitting on the cell membrane, and its role in glioblastoma has been largely overlooked.

Does this surface receptor also influence how tumor cells migrate and invade surrounding tissue? And could blocking it change their behavior?

slides.title: Activating GPER with estrogen or a targeted drug increased both migration and invasion in two glioblastoma cell lines.
slides.body:
Researchers tested U251 and U87 cells with estrogen, a GPER-specific activator called G-1, and a blocker called G-15. Both estrogen and G-1 ramped up cell migration and invasion, while G-15 reduced these effects whether used alone or combined with the activators.

GPER activation also pushed cells toward a mesenchymal-like state—a shape-shifting process associated with metastasis and treatment resistance in many cancers.

slides.title: This pathway could explain part of why sex hormones influence glioblastoma progression and survival.
slides.body:
If GPER signaling drives invasion and phenotype changes in human tumors the way it does in cultured cells, blocking it might slow disease spread. The receptor is already a drug target in other cancers.

Understanding how membrane and intracellular estrogen receptors work together—or compete—could open new combination strategies for one of the hardest cancers to treat.

caveats: This study used two cell lines grown in lab dishes, not tumors in living organisms or human patients.
The experiments did not track whether blocking GPER affects tumor growth or survival, only migration and invasion markers.

cta.headline: Curious how hormones shape cancer?
cta.sub: Follow for research that connects biology, behavior, and treatment—one study at a time.

caption: A receptor on the surface of glioblastoma cells responds to estrogen and appears to crank up their ability to migrate and invade, according to lab experiments in two human-derived cell lines. Researchers used a GPER agonist called G-1 and an antagonist called G-15 to isolate the receptor's effects, finding that activation promoted a mesenchymal-like phenotype linked to aggressive cancer behavior. Published in Cell Adhesion & Migration, the study worked with U251 and U87 cells under controlled conditions. Results in cultured cells don't guarantee the same dynamics occur in living tumors. Full study: doi.org/10.1080/19336918.2026.2720325—What brain tumor scares you most?
